1:
Where the ten years’ quiet came from, and how quiet. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) takes the rest as a result of Abijah’s great victory, the phrase being explained two verses later as having no war in those years, and the interval spent strengthening the defences of the country. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) presses the dependence harder: Abijah’s victory laid the foundation of a peace that was the reward of Asa’s piety and reformation, so that though Abijah had little religion himself he prepared the way for one that had much; had he not quieted the land, Asa could not have reformed it, for amid the din of arms the voice of law is unheard. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) qualifies the word, allowing no open war but private hostilities between Asa’s subjects and Baasha’s. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) reports the reckoning that counts the ten years from the fifth of the reign to the fifteenth.

What the commendation amounts to is measured carefully. Henry breaks it into three, that Asa aimed at pleasing God and studied to approve himself to him, that he saw God’s eye always upon him, which helped much to keep him to what was good, and that God graciously accepted him; happy are those who walk by this rule, to do what is right not in their own eyes, nor in the eye of the world, but in the eyes of God. Ellicott reads the Hebrew as the good and the right, an expression the next two verses define and one used later of Hezekiah. Clarke narrows it to the law’s requirement about worship, Asa being no idolater though, morally speaking, not exempt from faults. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) note how much the parallel in Kings leaves out, recording only the length of the reign, the removal of the idols, and a lifelong devotion that left the high places standing.

What was pulled down, and what was left standing, is itemised. Ellicott renders the phrase altars of the alien, and observes that the summary in Kings about taking away all the idols his fathers had made is here expanded into details, though the chronicler omits the temple prostitutes that Kings names; of the images he prefers shattered the pillars, obelisks of a kind dedicated to Baal and symbolising the solar rays. Keil and Delitzsch identify the same objects as sun-pillars consecrated to Baal as sun-god, erected near or upon his altars. John Gill (reformed) traces the altars to a strange people, the Zidonians, Ammonites and Moabites, surviving from the time of Solomon, who built them for his wives; and he reads the images as sun images, made in the form of the sun, or dedicated to it, or temples for it. Ellicott adds the limit that matters: it is clear from two later notices that the high places dedicated to the worship of Jehovah were not done away with.

The command to the people, and the oversight under which they rested, closes the account. Henry notices the division of labour, that since the priests attended God’s altars Asa obliged the people to do their part, requiring them to seek the God of their fathers and not the gods of the heathen and to observe all divine institutions, which many had neglected; and though they were much in love with their idols and very loth to leave them, the convictions of their consciences sided with the commands of Asa, so that they could not for shame refuse. He turns this into counsel for magistrates, that those who use power vigorously against profaneness meet less opposition than they feared, vice being a sneaking thing. Gill specifies the means, that Asa did it by a public edict, requiring prayer to God and him only. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch agree that quiet before him means peace enjoyed under his oversight.
6:
What the building was for, and how far. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) states the purpose plainly, to preserve his territories from invasion and strengthen the kingdom’s frontiers. John Gill (reformed) names the quarter feared, a defence against Israel and other nations as Rehoboam had made before him, and suggests these were works Shishak may have demolished. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) admits the names of the cities are unknown and warns against the obvious guess, since Geba and Mizpah were fortified by Asa only after the war with Baasha; what is indicated is rather a general system of defence like Rehoboam’s, who fortified fifteen cities. He notices too that the word for bars, elsewhere singular, is plural here, and reads the close as meaning they built prosperously, without let or hindrance. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) dwells instead on the rest itself: those have rest indeed to whom God gives rest, and peace indeed to whom Christ gives peace.

One clause is re-punctuated with consequences. Ellicott takes the land being yet before them to mean open to them, free from hostile occupation, a phrase borrowed from Genesis, and notes a masculine pronoun where a feminine belongs, probably a clerical error. He would omit the word while and put a stop at bars, making it a statement rather than a condition: the land is still before us, for we have sought the Lord. Gill adds only that the speech was to the nobles and principal men. Wesley turns the same clause into experience, that it is good to seek the Lord, since while we pursue the world we meet with nothing but vexation.

The two armaments are distinguished, and the arithmetic doubted. Ellicott makes Judah’s the large shield and lance and Benjamin’s the short or round shield, so that the men of Judah were the hoplites, or heavy-armed, the Benjaminites the light-armed, or peltasts as a Greek writer would say. Clarke guesses at their make, targets with the dagger in the centre and javelins for distant fight, and observes the second body were not only archers but carried shield and sword for close fight. On the total of five hundred and eighty thousand Ellicott holds the entire male population capable of bearing arms must be included, a standing army of that strength being unthinkable, and finds Benjamin’s proportion much too high, though that tribe was always famous for warriors. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) read the muster as a foil, recorded only to show that Asa set his hope of victory not on the strength of his army but on the all-powerful help of the Lord. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) takes the practical lesson, that he now found the benefit of having an army already raised, since provision we thought needless may soon appear of great advantage.

Who the invader was is the hardest question. Ellicott identifies Zerah with Osorchon the Second, who succeeded Shishak as king of Egypt, and reads the expedition as an attempt to bring Judah again under the Egyptian yoke, since Shishak had made Rehoboam tributary while Asa had restored the defences and reorganised his fighting material, steps indicating a desire for independence. Keil and Delitzsch report the usual identification with Osorchon the First of the Bubastitic dynasty, but also the objection that Zerah was an Ethiopian and no Egyptian prince, who marched through Egypt as a conqueror under Takeloth. Clarke places him in the Ethiopia south of Egypt near Libya, whose people are joined with his elsewhere, and doubts the distance, since from far off such an army could not have found forage. Wesley prefers the Arabian, the Hebrew word being commonly so used and those peoples nearer. Gill weighs both and decides for Africa, since the host included Libyans. Of the number Ellicott says it is out of all proportion to the three hundred chariots, which looks correct.
10:
Where the armies met cannot be fixed. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) admits the valley is not identified and reports the Greek reading, the ravine north of Mareshah, which would require changing a single letter in the Hebrew, while the Syriac and Arabic have the wady of Mareshah. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) reject the identification commonly proposed and hold only that it lay nearer Mareshah, west or north-west. John Gill (reformed) marks the courage of the advance, that Asa went out against him notwithstanding so great an army, and places the prayer before the battle, at the head of the army and for its encouragement. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) draws the connection with the years of quiet, that he who sought God in his peace and prosperity could with holy boldness cry to him in his trouble and call him his God; the prayer is short, he adds, but has much in it.

The central clause is contested word by word. Keil and Delitzsch render it, none is with Thee to help between a mighty one and a weak, meaning that none but God can help in an unequal battle, that is, help the weaker side; they note that the Latin took it instead to mean it makes no difference whether he helps with few or many, but hold the passage usually cited for that sense is differently worded and so no standard here. Ellicott reaches much the same rendering, finding the construction paralleled in Genesis; the alternative that makes it mean whether strong or powerless he judges Rabbinic rather than ancient usage. He calls very plausible a proposal to read retain strength for help, giving: it is not for any to withstand thee, whether strong or powerless. Of the Syriac he says it is more like a Targum than a translation, evading the difficulty rather than explaining it.

What Asa was asking, two further ways. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) hears the sentiment Jonathan uttered before the garrison, and gives the Targum: help us, because we depend on thy Word, and in its name we come against this great host. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) presses the last petition, that if the enemy prevails against us he prevails as it were against thee, because thou art our God, and we go forth in thy name. Henry breaks it into four pleas and puts the first most sharply: we do not say, Lord, take our part, for we have a good army for thee to work by, but take our part, for without thee we have no power. Ellicott adds the lexical notes: rest means rely, we go is we are come, and the word for multitude is that used of Jeroboam’s army, usually denoting an armed host.

The rout and the plunder. Keil and Delitzsch follow the flight to Gerar, the old Philistine city whose ruins lie three leagues south-south-east of Gaza, and render the result, there fell of the Cushites so that to them was not revival, so many that they could not make a stand again. Ellicott prefers survival to revival, calls the phrase a vivid hyperbole, and reads before his host as before his camp, since Asa’s army is the Lord’s; of the cities round Gerar he supposes they had helped Zerah, and notes the word for spoil here is a late one where the next verse has a classical term. Clarke accounts for the quantity by position, these cities lying in the rear of the army and having laid up much forage; the discomfiture was great, he says, because God fought for the people, though a million of men in one place is almost too much to conceive. Gill reads the tents of cattle as people who dwelt in tents for the pasturage; Henry closes that the wealth of the sinner is laid up for the just.
